# variables 
POLY_ID : Census Block Group ID
MEDHVAL : Median value of all owner occupied housing units
PCTBACHMOR : Proportion of residents in Block Group with at least a bachelor's degree
PCTVACANT : Proportion of housing units that are vacant
PCTSINGLES : Percent of housing units that are detached single family houses
NBELPOV100: Number of households with incomes below 100% poverty level (i.e., number of households living in poverty)
MEDHHINC : Median household income

```{r}
# check if any of the data have any zero values

sapply(regression_data[c("MEDHVAL", "PCTBACHMOR",
                         "PCTVACANT", "PCTSINGLES", "NBELPOV100")],
       function(x) sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
# use the log command to create 5 new variables 

LNMEDHVAL <- log(MEDHVAL)
LNPCTBACHMOR <- log(1+PCTBACHMOR)
LNNBELPOV100 <- log(1+NBELPOV100)
LNPCTVACANT <- log(1+PCTVACANT)
LNPCTSINGLES <- log(1+PCTSINGLES)
```

```{r}
# view the histograms of the new variables 

hist(LNMEDHVAL)
hist(LNPCTBACHMOR)
hist(LNNBELPOV100)
hist(LNPCTVACANT)
hist(LNPCTSINGLES)
```
Note that the dependent variable does look more or less normal
after the transformation – hence, LNMEDHVAL will be used as
the dependent variable in the regression analysis. You will also
see that for the predictors, the logarithmic transformation only
helps normalize the NBELPOV100 variable (so we will use
LNNBELPOV100 in the subsequent analyses). The other
variables have a large spike at zero (i.e., zero-inflated
distributions) after the transformations, so we will use the
original, untransformed PCBACHMORE, PCTVACANT, and
PCTSINGLES variables in the regression

```{r}
# determine if the relationship between the dependent variables and each of the predictors is linear, create four scatter plots

plot(LNMEDHVAL,LNNBELPOV100)
plot(LNMEDHVAL,PCTBACHMOR)
plot(LNMEDHVAL,PCTVACANT)
plot(LNMEDHVAL,PCTSINGLES)
```

```{r}
# check the Pearson correlations between all of the predictors

cor(cbind(PCTVACANT, PCTSINGLES, PCTBACHMOR, LNNBELPOV100))
```
Note whether you observe severe multicollinearity, and whether it’s appropriate to include all 4 variables as predictors.

None of the variables show severe multicollinearity. The most severe result is -0.3197668.

```{r}
# regression analysis 

regression <- lm(LNMEDHVAL ~ PCTVACANT + PCTSINGLES + PCTBACHMOR + LNNBELPOV100, data = regression_data)

regression
```

```{r}
# summary table

summary(regression)
```

```{r}
# ANOVA table

anova(regression)
```

```{r}
regression_predicted <- fitted(regression)
regression_residuals <- residuals(regression)
regression_standardresiduals <- rstandard(regression)

regression_predicted
regression_residuals
regression_standardresiduals
```

```{r}
# scatter plot of standardized residuals 

plot(
  regression_predicted,
  regression_standardresiduals,
  xlab = "Predicted Values",
  ylab = "Standardized Residuals",
  main = "Standardized Residuals vs. Predicted Values",
  pch = 20
)

abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

```{r}
# stepwise regression

step_regression <- stepAIC(regression, direction = "both")
step_regression
step_regression$anova
AIC(step_regression)
```

The stepwise regression procedure using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) selected the initial model as the final model. All four predictors—PCTVACANT, PCTSINGLES, PCTBACHMOR, and LNNBELPOV100—were retained because removing any individual predictor increased the AIC. The full model had an AIC of -3448.16, the lowest among the models evaluated. Therefore, the procedure did not identify an improvement by removing any of the predictors.

```{r}
# k fold validation 
regression_data$LNNBELPOV100 <- LNNBELPOV100
cv1 <- CVlm(
  data = regression_data,
  form.lm = formula(regression),
  m = 5,
  plotit = FALSE
)

# format
# Create plot data
plot_data <- data.frame(
  Observed = cv1$LNMEDHVAL,
  Predicted = cv1$cvpred,
  Fold = factor(cv1$fold)
)

# Assign a different color to each fold
fold_colors <- c("steelblue", "tomato", "forestgreen", "orange", "purple")

# Leave space on the right for the legend
par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 10), xpd = TRUE)

# Plot observed versus predicted values
plot(
  plot_data$Observed,
  plot_data$Predicted,
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.6,
  col = fold_colors[as.numeric(plot_data$Fold)],
  xlab = "Observed log median housing value",
  ylab = "Cross-validated predicted value",
  main = "5-Fold Cross-Validation",
  bty = "l"
)

# Reference line for perfect predictions
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "gray40")

# Legend on the right
legend(
  "topright",
  inset = c(-0.65, 0),
  legend = c(paste("Fold", 1:5), "Perfect prediction"),
  col = c(fold_colors, "gray40"),
  pch = c(rep(16, 5), NA),
  lty = c(rep(NA, 5), 2),
  lwd = c(rep(NA, 5), 2),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.8
)

par(xpd = FALSE)


rmse1 <- sqrt(mean(
  (cv1$LNMEDHVAL - cv1$cvpred)^2,
  na.rm = TRUE
))

rmse1
```

```{r}
# second cross validation 

# Create the second regression model with only two predictors
regression2 <- lm(
  LNMEDHVAL ~ PCTVACANT + MEDHHINC,
  data = regression_data
)

# Run 5-fold cross-validation
cv2 <- CVlm(
  data = regression_data,
  form.lm = formula(regression2),
  m = 5,
  plotit = FALSE
)

# Format the cross-validation results
plot_data <- data.frame(
  Observed = cv2$LNMEDHVAL,
  Predicted = cv2$cvpred,
  Fold = factor(cv2$fold)
)

# Assign a different color to each fold
fold_colors <- c("steelblue", "tomato", "forestgreen", "orange", "purple")

# Leave space on the right for the legend
par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 10), xpd = TRUE)

# Plot observed versus predicted values
plot(
  plot_data$Observed,
  plot_data$Predicted,
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.6,
  col = fold_colors[as.numeric(plot_data$Fold)],
  xlab = "Observed log median housing value",
  ylab = "Cross-validated predicted value",
  main = "5-Fold Cross-Validation: PCTVACANT + MEDHHINC",
  bty = "l"
)

# Reference line for perfect predictions
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "gray40")

# Legend on the right
legend(
  "topright",
  inset = c(-0.65, 0),
  legend = c(paste("Fold", 1:5), "Perfect prediction"),
  col = c(fold_colors, "gray40"),
  pch = c(rep(16, 5), NA),
  lty = c(rep(NA, 5), 2),
  lwd = c(rep(NA, 5), 2),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.8
)

par(xpd = FALSE)

# Calculate RMSE
rmse2 <- sqrt(mean(
  (cv2$LNMEDHVAL - cv2$cvpred)^2,
  na.rm = TRUE
))

rmse2
```

## INTRODUCTION (Sara)
In this analysis, we examined the relationship between Philadelphia median house values and several neighborhood characteristics using census block-level data. We measured the relationship by regressing median house value on the following variables: 

*Proportion of residents in Block Group with at least a bachelor’s

*Proportion of housing units that are vacant

*Percent of housing units that are detached single family houses

*Number of households with incomes below 100% poverty level (i.e., number of households living in poverty)

*Median household income

The regression output tells us (rate of significance, association). A 1 unit increase is associated with an xx increase of xx (slope). The p-value for xx demonstrates that xx (for each variable). The null hypothesis is tha the predictor has not association with our dependent variable. Because our Do we fail to reject the null? 

Peer-reviewed studies suggest a positive relationship between median house value and median household income, and neighborhoods with clustered college graduates (Harvard University, US Census, National Bureau of Economic Research) . We want to examine a broader set of variables and their relationship to median house value. 

Historically, single-family homes are clustered in areas with higher median house value. Starting in the 1930s, racist redlining and zoning practices became commonplace across the country, with the intention of maintaining segregated neighborhoods, denying Black and brown families a path to generational wealth accumulation, and displacing historically Black and brown neighborhoods. As a result, white and wealthy neighborhoods, typically with a large concentration of single-family homes, higher rates of education, and higher median household income, were protected from harmful redevelopment such as highways bisecting communities and eminent domain of homes and businesses. Meanwhile, Black and brown communities were subject to significant displacement and deliberately denied access to homeownership and property value appreciation, the effects of which we still see today. Although race is not a variable in our model, Philadelphia’s history of redlining and Urban Renewal contributed to the economically stratified neighborhood patterns we see in this model. The history of redlining and displacement does not disaggregate race from class; in fact, these policies were racist precisely because of their targeted classism. Policies such as redlining and urban renewal were framed as economic revitalization initiatives, but in practice, they resulted in the disinvestment of Black and brown neighborhoods, making poor neighborhoods poorer and wealthy neighborhoods wealthier. The predictors we evaluate are likely related to our response variable because they stem from the same historical processes that shaped Philadelphia and much of our country.

## DISCUSSION & LIMITATIONS (Sara)

To recap, we developed a linear regression model in which median house value was regressed on five independent variables. We attempted to determine a relationship by testing if the null hypothesis, xx, was rejected or a failure to reject… We did this through following the following steps: 
We found the mean and standard deviation of the dependent variable and each predictor
We plotted histograms of the dependent variable and each predictor to determine whether the variables were normally distributed. None of them were, more specifically, they were all right skewed, so we performed logarithmic transformations on each to  determine their transformed histogram shape. The logarithmic transformation helped in creating a normally distributed histogram for the dependent variable and one predictor (NBELPOV100). It did not help because they have a large spike at zero (zero-inflated distributions) so we used the original for these variables. 
We then created scatter plots to determine if there was any severe multicollinearity. We determined no severe multicollinearity was present. 
We then created a map of the transformed median house value and split the values into 


The final model includes all 4 predictors. We The RMSE was xx, in the 5-fold with xx. The R^2 and adjusted R^2 were xx and xx, almost identical because xx. This tells us that we have a reasonably good model because it demonstrates that our independent variable account for xx% of the variance we see in the dependent variable?? 

Using raw numbers for households living in poverty may not provide the most accurate representation of rates of poverty in Philadelphia block groups. Two very different-sized block groups can have the same raw number of households living in poverty. By using this data, we don’t see the relationship between block group size and rate of households in poverty, we would only see that two block groups have the same raw number of households in poverty. By using percentage, we would see the proportion of households living in poverty per block group. 


It would not make sense to run a Ridge or LASSO regression here because these methods are intended to be used on models with severe multicollinearity or a proportionally high number of variables relative to the number of observations. Both methods penalize large coefficients to reduce variance and overfitting. The Ridge regression shrinks and retains every variable, which makes the model less sensitive to individual data points. The LASSO regression may shrink some variables to zero, completely dropping them from the model if they are redundant or ineffective. Because we did not see severe multicollinearity (the most severe r value was -.32) and we have 1,700 observations with only xx variables, we determined that using a Ridge or Lasso method would not be effective in making our model more predictive and may make our coefficients harder to interpret.
